films.title: Kettle
article: Kettle was shot over twenty-six days in a coastal town in Northumberland during the spring of 2022. Cinematographer Marten Hollis photographed the film on 35mm using an Arricam LT, with Cooke S4 lenses for most interiors.

The production avoided Steadicam entirely, relying on a dolly and handheld work in the cramped kitchen set. A dented kettle, bought at a flea market in Hexham, became the film's central prop. The glowing LED panels on the futuristic fridge in the dream sequence were built by the art department as props.

films.title: Overpass
article: Overpass was filmed beneath the Leeds inner ring road over five weeks in autumn 2021. The film was shot digitally and framed for 2.39:1, the widest frame director Dario Fenwick had used.

films.title: Marrow: A Winter Account
article: Marrow: A Winter Account was filmed in the Tatra foothills in February 2019. The film was shot on Eastman Double-X black-and-white negative, using an Arricam ST.

Director Agnieszka Thorvald had originally intended to shoot in colour on Kodak Vision3 500T, but changed her mind after seeing tests of the village at dusk. The film was composed for a 1.33:1 frame. Some accounts suggest a Hawk anamorphic lens was used for the dream sequence.
A later home-media release was letterboxed to 1.66:1 in some territories.

films.title: Dovetail
article: Dovetail was shot on 35mm in a disused joinery in Suffolk. The title refers to the dovetail joint that the protagonist teaches her son to cut.

films.title: Cradle of Wolves
article: Cradle of Wolves was framed for 1.66:1, as it had been on The Weight of Gulls.

films.title: Little Engines
article: Little Engines combines live action with miniature railway sets built at a model workshop in Derby. Principal photography used the RED Komodo, which the production chose for its size inside the miniatures.

films.title: Sundial
article: Sundial was filmed in a walled garden in Kent over twenty days in the summer of 2023. Brandvold avoided artificial light outdoors and never used a drone, despite early storyboards that showed the garden from above.

films.title: Tin Crown
article: Tin Crown was shot in a scrapyard outside Rotterdam, mostly in daylight. The film was presented in 1.85:1, though early festival screenings used a 2.39:1 crop that Krull later disowned.

pages.title: Kettle: Marten Hollis on the warmth of 35mm
paragraphs: Marten Hollis had wanted to shoot on film since he first read Ines Volkaert's script for Kettle. Together they chose Kodak Vision3 500T for the interiors and Kodak Vision3 250D for the few exteriors on the harbour.

Q: Did you test digital at all? Hollis: We shot a day of tests on an ARRI Alexa Mini alongside the film camera, but it was never a serious contender. The negative was processed at Cinelab and scanned at 4K, while the grade was done at Company 3 with Sami Kaltenbrunn. Somewhere along the way we also borrowed a Zeiss Ultra Prime set from a friend, though I'm not sure it was ever on the camera.

Most of the light in the flat came through the windows, supplemented with tungsten units bounced off the ceiling. Everyone asks about the kettle itself, which sat in nearly every shot; it was a cheap enamel one, and there was no trick to making it steam. In the scenes at Moira's bedside we used practicals, probably around 60-watt bulbs, although I honestly can't remember the exact wattage.
On Gannet Point, his previous feature, Hollis had leaned heavily on a Technocrane for the cliff-top scenes. There was no room for that kind of equipment in Kettle, and he never used a crane on it.

pages.title: Domestic Tension: Kettle
paragraphs: For Kettle, Hollis and Volkaert framed for 1.85:1, a choice the director describes as “the shape of a doorway.” The streaming release, however, presents the film at 1.78:1 to fill television screens.

The filmmakers had planned to shoot the flashbacks on Super 16 but abandoned the idea when the camera package fell through, and the flashbacks were instead photographed on the same 35mm stock through a Black Pro-Mist filter.
Unlike Gannet Point, Kettle was finished with a photochemical ENR step on its archival print.

Hollis credits his mentor, the documentary cameraman Piet Varga, with the habit of always carrying ND filters, which most cinematographers of Varga's generation shared. Varga shot almost everything on an Arriflex 416 in his later years. A kettle whistles over the opening credits, and Hollis wanted the image to feel equally insistent.

pages.title: Gannet Point: Marten Hollis on the edge
paragraphs: Gannet Point, Corran Aske's windswept thriller, was shot on the Alexa Mini LF with Panavision Primo lenses. Hollis framed the film in 2.39:1.

Q: The cliff-top sequences are vertiginous. How were they done? Hollis: Mostly on a Technocrane parked forty feet from the edge, with Lys Petrakova operating remotely. We talked about using a drone, but the wind on that headland would have thrown it into the sea.

Hollis grew up in Sunderland and began as a clapper loader on television documentaries. His first credits as cinematographer were music videos shot on Super 8 and a Canon C300 Mark II borrowed from a college friend.
For the night interiors of the lighthouse, the electrical team rigged Astera tubes inside the lantern room.

pages.title: Colorist Sami Kaltenbrunn on grain, film-out and The Tollkeepers
paragraphs: Sami Kaltenbrunn has spent the past three years at Company 3 in London, where his recent credits include the series The Tollkeepers and the features Kettle and Gannet Point.

Q: Kettle was shot on film. What did you do in the grade? Kaltenbrunn: Very little. The negative already had the texture, so we did not add any grain, and we built a single LUT from the dailies that carried through to the end.

Q: And Gannet Point? Kaltenbrunn: That was the opposite problem, because it was digital and Corran wanted it to feel like a 1970s print, so we added grain in the grade and did a film-out for the festival copy.
On The Tollkeepers, which shot on the Sony Venice 2, Kaltenbrunn simulated anamorphic flares in the grade because the producers had ruled out real anamorphic glass.
Q: Is there a look you keep returning to? Kaltenbrunn: Most colorists I trained with would reach for a bleach bypass emulation whenever a director said 'gritty', and I try hard not to.

pages.title: Ines Volkaert on 'Kettle' and the Art of the Small Room
paragraphs: Ines Volkaert's second feature premiered in Karlovy Vary to warm reviews.
The director spoke about casting non-professionals from the town.
Cinematographer Marten Hollis shot the film on 35mm.

pages.title: How 'Overpass' Found Beauty Under the Motorway
paragraphs: Dario Fenwick's Overpass takes place almost entirely in the shadow of a ring-road flyover, and cinematographer Lusine Arkady wanted the concrete to feel enormous. She shot the film on the ARRI Alexa 35 with a set of Atlas Orion anamorphics, framing for 2.39:1.

“We never used a crane,” Arkady says. “Everything is from the height of a person standing on the pavement.” For the long walks along the hard shoulder, Benedek Saar operated a Steadicam, which let the camera keep pace with the traffic.

Night exteriors relied on the sodium streetlights already on the overpass, supplemented by Creamsource Vortex8 units on lifts dialled to match. Arkady had hoped to use Kodak Vision3 500T for the night work, but the budget could not stretch to film and the idea was dropped in pre-production.
The LED panels that flicker on the lorry's dashboard were added by the art department and play as part of the scenery.

pages.title: Lusine Arkady: Concrete and Bloom
paragraphs: Lusine Arkady began her career shooting car commercials in France, and on one of them a gimbal shot drifted beneath a motorway overpass in Lyon for nearly a minute.

On Overpass she worked almost exclusively with natural light during the day. Her follow-up, Static Bloom, was a different animal: a studio picture set in a vast greenhouse, shot on the Sony Venice 2 with Leica Summilux-C lenses.

Q: Did any of the Overpass approach carry over? Arkady: The handheld language, yes. We used handheld for every scene inside the greenhouse. Arkady: There may be one or two drone shots in there; the producers had a unit out on the last week.

Arkady says that, had Static Bloom been shot on 65mm as the studio first suggested, the greenhouse would have looked like a postcard. The Alexa 65 is, she notes, capable of extraordinary detail in foliage, but she has never owned or rented one.

pages.title: Steadicam Operator Benedek Saar on Walking With Actors
paragraphs: Benedek Saar has operated Steadicam on more than thirty features, most recently Overpass and Anselm Okafor's Northbound Choir.

Q: What rig do you fly these days? Saar: I own a Steadicam M-2 Volt now, but on Northbound Choir I was still on the older sled, and half the choir scenes ended up on a gimbal anyway because the church aisles were too narrow.

Q: Overpass has those long walks by the motorway. Saar: Those were the hardest days of my life, honestly, with lorries passing a metre from the lens and the wind pulling at the sled. Saar: We put an ND filter on to hold the shutter where Lusine wanted it.
Saar: People think Steadicam operators all want the camera to float, but most of the old-school operators I learned from actually preferred a dolly whenever the floor allowed it.

pages.title: Growing the greenhouse of Static Bloom
paragraphs: Static Bloom's greenhouse was a partial set at Bray, extended digitally by the effects team under supervisor Ravi Lindgaard.
The flowers that open in time-lapse were entirely CG, lit by virtual HMI sources matched to the set's real lighting plan. On set, the crew lit the greenhouse with SkyPanels hung above the glass roof.
For the shot that tracks through a single petal, the team built a virtual camera with a simulated split diopter so the bee and the actor's eye could both hold focus.
Lindgaard notes that a real split diopter was tested on set but did not make the final cut.

pages.title: Tobiah Rensch on the Night Shifts of 'Lantern'
paragraphs: Thandiwe Morrow's Lantern follows a night-shift nurse through a single winter, and cinematographer Tobiah Rensch shot it on 16mm with an Arriflex 416. Kodak describes Vision3 500T as its most versatile tungsten-balanced stock.

The Film Stage: Was there ever a digital version of this film? Rensch: There was a moment where the financiers wanted it on the RED Komodo, and we shot a test day with it, but Thandiwe hated it and we went back to film.

The Film Stage: The hospital corridors glow. Rensch: That's mostly the existing fluorescent fittings, with Kino Flos tucked into the ceiling where a tube had died. Rensch: I think the second unit carried a Steadicam for the car park, but I wasn't there.

In one dream sequence, Mara walks past a row of paper lanterns strung over a street market, and Rensch filmed it at magic hour to let the lanterns glow against the dusk. The lantern of the title is a battered camping lamp Mara carries, and in close-ups its glow was boosted with a small LiteMat hidden behind it.

pages.title: Below Deck: Tobiah Rensch on Pilgrim Tide
paragraphs: Nadira Voss's Pilgrim Tide reunites her with cinematographer Tobiah Rensch, who last year shot Lantern. Just as on Lantern, Rensch shot Pilgrim Tide on 16mm, this time with Zeiss Super Speed lenses.
Q: Pilgrim Tide is mostly at sea. Rensch: We were on a fishing trawler for eleven days, all handheld, because a gimbal would have been useless on a deck that was pitching ten degrees.
Rensch: On Lantern we had a dolly for the corridors, but on the trawler there was nowhere to lay track.
The film was graded at Light Iron, and the 16mm negative was later scanned at 4K for the archive master.

pages.title: Pilgrim Tide: Light on the Water
paragraphs: Rensch lit the trawler's cabin almost entirely with practicals, swapping the boat's fittings for warmer bulbs. A few pickups were reportedly shot later on a digital camera, though the article's sources disagree.
For the storm night, the second unit hung an HMI from the harbour crane to suggest a lighthouse beam sweeping the deck.
Rensch says the film might have been shot on 35mm had the trawler's cabin been large enough for an Arricam ST.
In a sidebar, Rensch recalls that on Lantern the hospital set was lit with Astera tubes as well as the existing fixtures.

pages.title: Lantern
paragraphs: Cinesite provided 96 invisible effects shots for Thandiwe Morrow's Lantern, supervised by Ravi Lindgaard.
Snowfall in the car park was added digitally and lit in CG to match the sodium practicals visible in the 16mm plates.
The studio's work may also have included cleanup on shots photographed with a drone, according to one crew listing.

pages.title: The Lantern Keepers
paragraphs: The Lantern Keepers is an eight-part fantasy series for which Cinesite created a lighthouse city and its flying ships.
The series was shot on the ARRI Alexa 65 at a studio in Montreal, with Cinesite supervising on set.
Flying-ship plates were captured with a Technocrane against blue screen.

pages.title: How 'Wait… Then Run' Kept Its Camera Moving
paragraphs: In “Wait… Then Run,” Halvard Mung's chase thriller, cinematographer Celeste Ourada keeps the camera moving for nearly the whole running time. Ourada shot on the RED V-Raptor, which she chose for its high frame rates, mounted on a Libra head for the car-to-car sequences.
“We decided against anamorphic early on,” she says. “The chase needed edges you could trust.” Spherical Zeiss Supreme Prime lenses were used throughout, and the film was framed for 2.00:1.

The Sony Venice 2, which the producers had suggested, offers an 8.6K full-frame sensor, according to Sony. Some reports say parts of the finale were shot on a Technocrane, though Ourada declined to confirm it.
Ourada's previous film, the documentary short Ferrymen, was shot entirely on a Blackmagic Pocket.

pages.title: Wait... Then Run
paragraphs: Cinesite delivered 212 shots for Halvard Mung's Wait Then Run, working closely with production VFX supervisor Ivo Brennan-Saito.
The highway pile-up was built as a full CG environment, rendered through a virtual camera whose movement was keyed to the real Libra head data.

Digital lighting artists relit the burning lorry with CG tungsten sources to match the plates. The team also added simulated anamorphic flares to the headlights at the director's request, though the film was shot with spherical lenses.
Cinesite's work on the film was completed in 2021 at its London studio.

pages.title: Jun Aldaine on grading Wait... Then Run and The Copper Season
paragraphs: Colorist Jun Aldaine graded both Wait... Then Run and The Copper Season at Company 3 in Toronto.
Q: How did you approach Wait... Then Run? Aldaine: Celeste gave me a show LUT she had built in prep, and we barely moved away from it.
Q: The Copper Season looks almost like a bleach bypass print. Aldaine: It does, but there was no lab process involved; that bleach bypass look is emulated digitally in the grade.
Aldaine: Ambrose shot The Copper Season on Kodak Vision3 250D, so a lot of that texture was already there.

pages.title: Northbound Choir: Celeste Ourada in the cold churches
paragraphs: Northbound Choir, Anselm Okafor's portrait of a touring youth choir, was photographed by Celeste Ourada, who previously shot Wait... Then Run. As with Wait... Then Run, Ourada used Zeiss Supreme Prime lenses, though this time on the Alexa Mini LF.

Q: How did you light the churches? Ourada: Natural light whenever we could, and LED panels bounced off the vaulting when the clouds came in. Ourada: There's a crane shot in one of my films that I'm still proud of.
Ourada studied photography in Lisbon before moving to London. Her graduation film was shot on a Bolex with Eastman Double-X black-and-white stock.
The choir's tour bus, its ceiling lined with decorative LED panels, was used as a moving location for the travel montages.

pages.title: Marrow: Yusuf Brennecke Goes Black-and-White
paragraphs: Marrow begins with a long shot of a woman pulling a sledge across a frozen field, and it never relents. Cinematographer Yusuf Brennecke shot the film on Eastman Double-X, with push processing of one stop for the night scenes.
Q: Why black-and-white? Brennecke: Agnieszka felt colour would make the snow pretty, so black-and-white was decided before I was even hired.
Brennecke: In the farmhouse we lit with tungsten and practicals, probably 100-watt household bulbs, though I couldn't swear to the wattage now.
Brennecke: The old masters would bounce a single HMI through the window, and that's what everyone of that era did.

pages.title: From Snow to Sand: Yusuf Brennecke
paragraphs: Yusuf Brennecke followed Marrow with Ash Meridian, a science-fiction drama shot in the Atacama.

Q: Ash Meridian is in colour and widescreen. Was that a reaction to Marrow? Brennecke: Partly. We shot Ash Meridian on the Alexa 65 with Hawk anamorphic lenses, which is about as far from Marrow as you can get.
Q: And the desert days? Brennecke: Huge negative fill, a Technocrane for the reveals and a lot of ND filters, because the sun there is merciless.

Q: Back to Marrow for a moment — was there any handheld? Brennecke: No handheld at all; every shot is on sticks or a dolly. Brennecke: There's one shot, I think, that was on 65mm, but I can't recall which film it ended up in.
Brennecke expects the next one will probably be on the ARRI Alexa 35, though nothing has been decided.

pages.title: Ash Meridian
paragraphs: Cinesite created the dust storms and orbital vistas of Ash Meridian under the supervision of Marguerite Oyelaran.
The orbital shots were composed with a virtual camera that mimicked the Hawk anamorphic lenses used on location, including their breathing and oval bokeh.
CG lighting for the station interior was built from HDRIs of the real set, which had been lit with SkyPanels and Creamsource Vortex8 fixtures.
The filmmakers had also tested a drone for the canyon flyovers, but those shots were ultimately replaced with fully CG versions.

pages.title: 'Ash Meridian' Ending Explained
paragraphs: The final ten minutes of Ash Meridian have divided audiences.
Director Kenji Abernathy discussed the station's fate.
Cinematographer Yusuf Brennecke described the last shot.

pages.title: Odile’s Garden: Noor Vellacott shoots a summer
paragraphs: Rémi Castagnol’s Odile’s Garden is a summer film, and Noor Vellacott shot it like one. The production used the Alexa Mini LF with Cooke Panchro Classic lenses, chosen for their soft fall-off.
Vellacott lit the garden almost entirely with natural light, shaping it with large frames of diffusion and the occasional HMI from the cherry picker.
Q: What about the greenhouse scene at night? Vellacott: That's Astera tubes laid along the planting beds, dimmed right down.
Q: You also shot Low Orchard the same year. Vellacott: Yes, and that one was all Super 16 on an Arriflex 416, a totally different discipline.
Odile, the character, keeps an old Super 8 camera in the potting shed, which she uses to film the bees.

pages.title: Low Orchard: Eighteen Days in Armagh
paragraphs: Low Orchard, Cormac Tierney-Bell's debut, was shot in eighteen days on Super 16 in County Armagh.
Unlike Odile's Garden, which she lit with HMIs, Vellacott lit Low Orchard with nothing but tungsten units and the occasional practical. Some sources claim the orchard finale used a gimbal.
The film was blown up from Super 16 to a 35mm film-out for its festival premiere, but its original 1.66:1 frame was preserved.
Tierney-Bell says he would have loved a Technocrane for the orchard finale but could never have afforded one.

pages.title: Noor Vellacott: Two Gardens
paragraphs: Noor Vellacott's two most recent features could hardly be more different.
On one, she used Black Pro-Mist filtration throughout; on the other she refused all diffusion.
Q: Which camera do you reach for first? Vellacott: Honestly, the Alexa Mini, though I haven't used it on a feature in years.
Vellacott shoots tests for every job on a RED Komodo she keeps at home, though none of that footage has ended up in a finished film.

pages.title: 'Salt and Cinder' DP Kasia Lindqvist on Shooting a Volcano
paragraphs: For “Salt and Cinder,” Fennimore Ruiz's volcanic-island western, Kasia Lindqvist shot on Kodak Vision3 250D and Kodak Vision3 500T with a Panavision Millennium XL2. Panavision says the Millennium XL2 is among the quietest 35mm cameras ever made.

“There's no drone in this film,” Lindqvist says flatly. “Every aerial is from a helicopter or the crane.” The production's equipment list, published in a trade paper, included Hawk anamorphic lenses, but it is unclear whether they were used.
The lab work was done at FotoKem, and the negative was finished through a digital intermediate.
Lindqvist had planned to shoot the cave sequences in VistaVision, but the cameras were booked by another production.

pages.title: Salt & Cinder
paragraphs: Cinesite's team completed 340 shots for Salt and Cinder, the bulk of them lava, ash and sky replacements.

The eruption's glow on the actors was real: the production rigged LED panels on the ground and programmed them with lava loops. In the fully CG wide shots, the lava itself served as the main light source in the render.
Cinesite added a faux split diopter to the duel's final shot so that both gunfighters stay sharp.
Oyelaran notes that the same approach had been used on Ash Meridian, where Cinesite also matched a virtual camera to real lens data.

pages.title: The gears of Hollow Clock
paragraphs: Hollow Clock, Emeric Sandoval-Hart's fable about a town where time runs backwards, relied on a mix of practical clockwork and CG.
VFX supervisor Ivo Brennan-Saito says the giant gears were shot in-camera using a Technocrane threaded through the miniature, then extended digitally.
The reverse-time shots were rendered with a CG camera that simulated a 65mm look, complete with digitally added grain.
For Wait... Then Run, Brennan-Saito had relied on Libra head data to match CG to the plates.

pages.title: Hollow Clock: Turning Back Time
paragraphs: For Hollow Clock, Kasia Lindqvist returned to digital, shooting on the Sony Venice 2 with Cooke S4 lenses.
Q: After Salt & Cinder, was it hard to leave film behind? Lindqvist: A little, but the Venice handles tungsten-lit interiors beautifully, and the clock tower set was almost all tungsten.
Lindqvist: The one thing I kept from Salt & Cinder was the bleach bypass look, which on Hollow Clock we only emulated with a LUT.
In the epilogue a character photographs the square with a Canon C300 Mark II, a prop the art department rented as dressing.

pages.title: Hollow Clock
paragraphs: Cinesite's Montreal studio contributed 150 shots to Hollow Clock, including the backwards-falling rain.
The rain was simulated in Houdini and lit with CG LED panels mirroring the set's real fixtures.
Plates were photographed on set with Cooke S4 lenses, whose distortion was profiled for the CG work.

pages.title: Half–Light Ferry: Ottoline Fairweather at sea
paragraphs: Mateus Corrigan’s Half–Light Ferry was shot aboard a working car ferry between Oban and Mull over three weeks in 2018. Ottoline Fairweather photographed it on 35mm with an Arricam LT, framing for 2.39:1. She tested Hawk anamorphic lenses against two other sets in prep, and the Hawks went on to shoot the whole film.
Key grip Bram Holloway built a sliding dolly track along the car deck. A Steadicam was considered for the stairwells but was never brought aboard.
Q: How much of the light is the ferry's own? Fairweather: Most of it; we replaced the strip lights in the lounge with Kino Flos of the same length, and the rest is the sea.
The film's 2023 4K restoration was supervised by Fairweather for its disc release.

pages.title: How Dovetail Kept 35mm Alive in a Joinery
paragraphs: Beatrix Holm's Dovetail is a carpentry drama, and its shooting schedule dovetailed awkwardly with Ottoline Fairweather's commitments on a commercial in Norway. Fairweather shot Dovetail on Kodak Vision3 500T using Zeiss Ultra Prime lenses.
Q: The workshop scenes have a wonderful dust in the air. Fairweather: That's a Black Pro-Mist 1/4 and a smoke machine, nothing clever. Fairweather: We had Astera tubes on the truck for weeks.
Fairweather: In Norway, the commercial was all drone and gimbal work, which is the opposite of how I like to shoot.

The joinery close-ups used a split diopter so that the dovetail joint and the carpenter's face could both be in focus. Continuing the process begun on Half-Light Ferry (2019), Fairweather had the Dovetail negative developed with an ENR step at the lab.
Holm says that if Dovetail had been shot on digital, the sawdust would have looked like noise. Holm hopes to shoot her next film on VistaVision.

pages.title: Ottoline Fairweather Looks Back
paragraphs: Ottoline Fairweather has shot five features, from Half-Light Ferry to Dovetail, and nearly all of them on film.
Q: Which of your films used IMAX? Fairweather: None of them used IMAX! People assume the ferry film did because of the horizon shots, but that was just 35mm anamorphic.
Fairweather: My first feature, which nobody has seen, was shot on a Canon C300 Mark II with a single zoom.
Fairweather: Somewhere in there we used a Technocrane, I think on the ferry film, but it might have been the other one.

pages.title: The Best Cinematography of 2023
paragraphs: Kettle (Marten Hollis): Shot on 35mm in a single flat, Ines Volkaert's film made a kitchen feel like a cathedral.
Odile's Garden (Noor Vellacott): Vellacott's Cooke Panchro Classic lenses gave the flowers a glow that no filter could.
Northbound Choir (Celeste Ourada): The choir's faces, lit by bounced LED panels in cold churches, are the year's most moving portraits.
Dovetail (Ottoline Fairweather): Fairweather's 500T night scenes in the workshop prove film is far from dead.
Vesper Street (Gideon Marsh-Okoro): Neon practicals and Hawk anamorphic glass made a single Glasgow block into a universe.
Pilgrim Tide (Tobiah Rensch): Shot handheld on a pitching trawler, it is the year's most physical film.

pages.title: The Copper Season: Ambrose Kettering remembers 1984
paragraphs: Wendell Akinyemi's The Copper Season is set during a mining strike in 1984, and cinematographer Ambrose Kettering wanted it to look like a photograph from that year. Kettering shot on Kodak Vision3 250D for the exteriors and pushed the 500T stock for night scenes at the pithead.

Q: What did you test in prep? Kettering: We tested a Black Pro-Mist and a set of Zeiss Super Speed lenses; the Super Speeds made it into the film, the filter did not. Kettering: The Kodak rep sent us some Eastman Double-X to play with too.
Kettering: A lot of my colleagues light miners' faces with a single LiteMat, but I used the helmet lamps the actors wore, with the bulbs swapped for brighter ones.
Kettering: The colliery's floodlights were period practicals, probably around 500 watts each, which we rewired to dimmers.

pages.title: Ambrose Kettering on the Backwards Road Trip of 'Signal Hill Road'
paragraphs: Tomasz Elling's Signal Hill Road is a road movie in reverse, starting at the destination. Ambrose Kettering, coming off The Copper Season, shot it on the ARRI Alexa 35 with Zeiss Supreme Prime lenses.
The Film Stage: After shooting film, did you miss it? Kettering: On The Copper Season we had Kodak; here we had a LUT that tried to remember Kodak.
The Film Stage: The car interiors are lit so naturally. Kettering: We had a Creamsource Vortex8 on a process trailer and some LED panels taped to the dashboard.
The drone shots over the coast were handled by aerial cinematographer Lio Fennick.
The road sign that gives the film its title was later reused in another feature, Fieldnote, where it appears in a crane shot.

pages.title: Flying the coast: Lio Fennick on Signal Hill Road
paragraphs: Lio Fennick has flown cameras over glaciers, stadiums and, most recently, the coastline in Signal Hill Road.

Q: What did you fly on Signal Hill Road? Fennick: An Alexa Mini on a heavy-lift drone, with a Zeiss Ultra Prime because it was light. Fennick: The production also hired an Alexa 65 for a week, but I only flew the Mini.
Fennick: For the night shots we tested a RED Komodo on a smaller rig, but none of it made the cut.
Fennick: Most aerial operators still prefer a gimbal-stabilised helicopter mount for anything over the sea, and I understand why.

pages.title: Tomasz Elling Sets 'Signal Hill Road' at Toronto
paragraphs: Tomasz Elling's third feature will premiere at Toronto.
The film reunites Elling with producer Hester Quayle.
Ambrose Kettering is the cinematographer.

pages.title: In 'Brine,' the Salt Ponds Do the Lighting
paragraphs: Saoirse Delacroix's Brine follows two sisters working the evaporation ponds of a failing salt works. The brine in the ponds turns pink in late summer, and cinematographer Pell Varady built the palette around it. The brine shrimp that give the ponds their colour were filmed for the opening by a macro unit using a Leica Summilux-C.
Varady shot on the Alexa Mini LF, with a set of Cooke Panchro Classic lenses detuned by the rental house.

“I never wanted to see a light in this film,” Varady says, “so there are no practicals at all, just the sky and some bounce.” Varady says the film may have a few shots where a Kino Flos was hidden in the salt sheds.
In an early draft of the shooting plan, the ponds were to be filmed entirely from a drone, but the plan was dropped before the shoot when the salt works banned flights.

pages.title: The Quarry Wives: Pell Varady in Granite and Silver
paragraphs: Delphine Arkwright's The Quarry Wives is set in a Cornish granite quarry in 1952, and Pell Varady shot it in black-and-white on Eastman Double-X.

Q: Was that a hard sell? Varady: Less than you'd think, because after Brine everyone knew I'd fight for it. Varady: On Brine I'd shot digital and we spent months in the grade at Light Iron; on The Quarry Wives the negative did most of the work.

Q: The quarry interiors are lit by lamps. Varady: The oil lamps are props; the real light is tungsten bouncing off the granite. Varady: The second unit probably used a zoom for the quarry wides, but I'd have to ask them.
Varady: The old studio cameramen would put an HMI up on the quarry rim; we didn't, but I thought about it. Varady says a sequel, if there is one, could be on 65mm.

pages.title: Gaffer Ruth Abernethy on windows and salt
paragraphs: Gaffer Ruth Abernethy has lit two very different films back to back: Kettle, a kitchen-sink drama shot in a flat, and Brine, shot on salt flats under an open sky.
Q: Kettle seems lit by the windows. Abernethy: It mostly was, plus SkyPanels outside two of the windows when the weather turned.
Q: And Brine? Abernethy: On Brine there was almost no lighting at all; my crew spent most days holding a 20-by-20 of muslin, though we did carry an HMI that never came off the truck.

Abernethy: My father was a gaffer too, and he swore by tungsten for skin tones, which is what most gaffers of his generation believed. Abernethy: There's a scene in one of them where we put a Creamsource Vortex8 on a cherry picker, but I honestly can't remember which film it was.

pages.title: Hamish Rudd on the 2 a.m. World of 'Pale Hours'
paragraphs: Ilse Marchetti's Pale Hours takes place between 2 and 5 a.m., and Hamish Rudd shot it on the Sony Venice 2 at high ISO.
The Film Stage: Were you tempted by film? Rudd: For about a week. We could have used Kodak Vision3 500T pushed two stops, but the grain would have eaten the faces.

Rudd: Instead we leaned on the city's own light, a few Astera tubes, maybe six or eight, hidden in doorways, and a lot of practicals. Rudd: There might be a Steadicam shot in the hospital, I honestly forget.
The Film Stage: There's a gorgeous shot through a split diopter in the laundromat. Rudd: That's actually two plates comped together; there was no diopter on the lens.
Rudd: The release was presented at 2.39:1 in cinemas, but we composed for 2.00:1 and the cinema version is a crop.

pages.title: 'Little Engines' DP Hamish Rudd on Shooting Miniature Trains
paragraphs: Orrin Paquette's Little Engines blends live action with miniature model railways, and Hamish Rudd shot both on the RED Komodo.
For the miniatures, Rudd used Zeiss Super Speed lenses with a Black Pro-Mist to soften the plastic edges.

“Paquette had wanted a VistaVision look for the trains,” Rudd recalls, “but in the end we simulated it by shooting tiny sensor crops and scaling up.” Paquette has said in other interviews that a Super 8 feel was achieved for the flashbacks, without saying how.
The Steadicam shots through the model village were achieved with a snorkel lens on a motion-control rig, not a Steadicam at all, despite what the press notes claimed.
Rudd shot the station-platform scenes at magic hour over three evenings.

pages.title: Hamish Rudd: Two Kinds of Night
paragraphs: Hamish Rudd was a camera operator for a decade before shooting Little Engines in 2020.
Q: Pale Hours and Little Engines are both night films in a way. Rudd: Yes, and both were lit with LED panels on dimmers, which you can do now in a way you couldn't ten years ago.
Q: Which one was harder? Rudd: On Little Engines we shot a camera test on 16mm, and Orrin loved it so much that the dream sequence ended up on 16mm.
Q: Do you have a favourite lens? Rudd: Probably the Zeiss Super Speed; I'd use it on everything if producers let me.

pages.title: The Weight of Gulls: Faisal Odelberg on the Shetland cliffs
paragraphs: Maren Solvik's The Weight of Gulls was shot on the Shetland coast in 2019 by Faisal Odelberg, who chose the ARRI Alexa Mini with Leica Summilux-C lenses.
Odelberg wanted the seabird colonies to feel overwhelming, so the second unit shot the cliffs with a long zoom from a boat.
Q: The interior of the croft feels like a painting. Odelberg: That's one window, a bounce, and a single tungsten Fresnel, probably a 2K, nothing more.
Odelberg: For the finale we had planned a Technocrane on the cliff, but the council refused permission and we went handheld instead.
The gulls' digital shadows in the storm sequence were added by the VFX team, who relit them with CG HMI sources.

pages.title: 'Cradle of Wolves' Cinematographer Faisal Odelberg Returns to Film
paragraphs: In “Cradle of Wolves,” Ysolde Brannigan's folk-horror fable, Faisal Odelberg returns to film after years of digital work. He shot Super 16 on an Arriflex 416 and graded at FotoKem.

“It's all fire, moonlight and HMIs bounced off white sheets,” Odelberg says of the forest nights. Odelberg's crew reportedly brought a Technocrane to the forest, although it is not clear if it was ever assembled.
For the wolf attack, the production considered a drone but chose a crane instead, since the animals panicked at the noise.
As with The Weight of Gulls, he used Leica Summilux-C lenses for the digital pickups shot a year later.

pages.title: Faisal Odelberg: Wind and Weather
paragraphs: Faisal Odelberg's two most recent features are linked by weather: both were shot in places where the wind never stops.
Q: On The Weight of Gulls, how did you keep the camera steady on the cliffs? Odelberg: A Libra head on a small crane, mostly, and sandbags.
Q: And on Cradle of Wolves? Odelberg: There it was the opposite; I wanted the wind in the frame, so it's all handheld and a little bit of Steadicam.

Odelberg: People ask me whether either film used diffusion; I think there was a diffusion filter on one of them for the dream scenes, but I'd have to check my notes. Odelberg: The next one, if it happens, might be shot in IMAX.

pages.title: One Day, One Garden: Shooting Sundial
paragraphs: Philippa Nkemelu's Sundial unfolds over a single day in a walled garden, with the sun's progress tracked by the stone sundial at its centre. Ilka Brandvold shot the film on the ARRI Alexa 35, using only natural light for every exterior.
Q: You must have had a strict schedule. Brandvold: We shot in story order, so magic hour really is the end of the film.

Brandvold: The sundial in the garden was a fibreglass prop; a real stone one would have been too heavy for the lawn. Brandvold: A replica sundial and a prop Arriflex 416 sit in the potting shed where the grandfather keeps his old things.

The film's lone interior was lit with a single SkyPanel through the window, set to match the angle of the sun at that hour. Rumours on set suggested a drone was flown for the opening, but Brandvold would not say.
ARRI advertises 17 stops of dynamic range for the Alexa 35, a figure Brandvold says she has never tested herself.

pages.title: Ironwood Lullaby: three generations on 35mm
paragraphs: Caspar Wendt's Ironwood Lullaby, a 2019 drama about a lumber family, was photographed by Ilka Brandvold on 35mm. Brandvold used Kodak Vision3 250D for the forest and Kodak Vision3 500T for the cabin interiors.
Q: You framed it at 1.85:1? Brandvold: Yes, though the streaming version was reframed to 2.00:1, which I never approved.

Brandvold: We'd planned some Super 8 inserts for the home movies but ended up shooting those on 35mm too and degrading them in the grade. Brandvold: I believe the cabin interiors had a diffusion filter too, but my notes from 2018 are lost.
Brandvold: The crane shot at the end, rising over the treeline, is the only time we used a crane.

pages.title: Ilka Brandvold: Time and Light
paragraphs: Ilka Brandvold's films are obsessed with time: Ironwood Lullaby spans three generations, Sundial a single day.
Q: Did you use any of the same gear? Brandvold: The Cooke S4 lenses, yes, on both films.
Q: And filtration? Brandvold: On Ironwood Lullaby, a 1/8 Black Pro-Mist; on Sundial nothing at all.
Brandvold: Somebody once told me Sundial would have looked better on 65mm, and maybe it would have. Brandvold: My mentor shot everything with a Panavision Primo zoom and never apologised for it.

pages.title: How 'Vesper Street' Turned One Glasgow Block Into a Neon Noir
paragraphs: Leona Iturbe's Vesper Street is a neon-lit noir set in a single block of Glasgow, and Gideon Marsh-Okoro shot it on the Sony Venice 2 with Hawk anamorphic lenses.

The neon signs that line the street are practicals built by the art department, and Marsh-Okoro used them as his key light. The street's bus shelters have advertising lightboxes made of LED panels, which were left as set dressing and switched off during most takes.

“We avoided handheld completely,” Marsh-Okoro says, “because the street had to feel like a stage.” Most of the film was shot on a dolly, with one Technocrane move over the rooftops at the end. One crew member recalled the production renting Leica Summilux-C lenses, but it is unclear for which scenes, if any.
The film was finished at Company 3 with a digital intermediate built around a show LUT.

pages.title: Tin Crown: Gideon Marsh-Okoro in the Scrapyard
paragraphs: Bastian Krull's Tin Crown is a children's fantasy about a scrap-metal king, shot by Gideon Marsh-Okoro on the ARRI Alexa Mini LF. Atlas markets the Orion series as the most affordable true anamorphic primes on the market.
Q: How different was it from Vesper Street? Marsh-Okoro: Completely. Vesper Street was all practicals and neon; Tin Crown is daylight and Kino Flos.
Marsh-Okoro: We did shoot one sequence with a gimbal on a bicycle, which I think is in the film, but Bastian may have cut it.

The crown itself was created as a CG prop in some scenes, lit by a virtual HMI rig in Houdini. Krull had wanted the junkyard scenes on 16mm, but the insurers wouldn't cover film cameras in the rain and the plan was dropped.

pages.title: Gideon Marsh-Okoro on rooftops and junkyards
paragraphs: Gideon Marsh-Okoro has shot two features in three years, plus a string of music videos.
Q: What was the most technically demanding thing you've done recently? Marsh-Okoro: Probably the rooftop sequence, which was a Technocrane on a rooftop in the rain.
Q: And the music videos? Marsh-Okoro: Those were mostly Blackmagic Pocket and a drone, whatever the budget allowed.
Marsh-Okoro: For the next feature I'm thinking about Atlas Orion lenses, but nothing is locked.

pages.title: Wren Calloway on the Birds of 'Fieldnote'
paragraphs: Aurelie Danso's Fieldnote follows an ornithologist cataloguing a disappearing marsh, and Wren Calloway shot it on Super 16 with an Arriflex 416.

The Film Stage: Did you use any artificial light? Calloway: Very little: a LiteMat in the hide, and the rest is the marsh at dawn. Calloway: We had ND filters with us, though in that light I'm not sure we ever needed them.
The Film Stage: There's a remarkable shot of starlings near the end. Calloway: That's a murmuration we got on the last day with a long zoom, completely by luck.

Calloway: In the field notes the character writes, she sketches a Leica Summilux-C she saw in a catalogue, which is a little joke from the art department. Calloway: Had we shot Fieldnote on digital, I think the birds would have looked like screensavers.

pages.title: Crosswind Bakery: Wren Calloway rises to fiction
paragraphs: Mikkel Ashdown's Crosswind Bakery, a gentle comedy set in a Faroese village bakery, was Wren Calloway's first narrative feature. Calloway shot on the Canon C300 Mark II with Zeiss Ultra Prime lenses, a package she knew from documentaries.
Q: The bakery glows. Calloway: The ovens did a lot of the work, along with tungsten practicals, probably 40-watt bulbs, that we swapped into the shop's own fittings.
Q: Was there any camera movement plan? Calloway: Mostly handheld, and one Steadicam shot following the bread van. Calloway: A friend lent us a gimbal, which may have ended up in one shot.
Calloway: My documentary mentor, Hauk Reinert, used to say you never need more than natural light and a reflector, and most of the Nordic doc crews still work that way.
The film was presented in 1.85:1 in cinemas and on its streaming release, matching the frame it was shot in.

pages.title: From Documentary to Fiction: Wren Calloway
paragraphs: Wren Calloway made the jump from documentary to fiction with Crosswind Bakery and followed it with Fieldnote four years later.
Calloway: On the bakery film we used a single Kino Flos unit over the counter for every scene.
Calloway: On Fieldnote I finally got to shoot film, and we processed at FotoKem.
Calloway: People always ask if one of them used an ENR or some lab trick, and the honest answer is that I don't remember.
Calloway: Some colleagues I admire shoot everything with a Black Pro-Mist; I've never used one.
